clue.text: Fit mock rings with unknown gems

indicators.note: to ring something is to circle it

parts.note: to mock is to jeer
fit and well: healthy
x, y and z are the algebraic unknowns

explanation.surface: A jeweller sneers at a tray of fake rings set with stones nobody can identify.
explanation.walkthrough: "Fit" and "mock" both read as adjectives in the surface, but mock is a verb (jeer) and fit means healthy.
explanation.definitionFit: Gems set in rings and necklaces are jewellery.

clue.text: Candy corporation trousers altered by Spooner

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the two words here trade first letters

parts.note: corporation is old slang for a paunch or belly; Spooner gives it the J of the other word
jeans are denim trousers; Spooner gives them the B of the other word

explanation.surface: A sweet company's trousers get changed by a man called Spooner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'corporation' looks like a company, but it is old British slang for a pot belly. Say BELLY JEANS and swap the B and J sounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Candy is the American word for sweets, and jelly beans are small chewy sweets.

clue.text: Nuns use these glues regularly to stop drips

indicators.note: to stop is to plug, so the picked letters go inside the drips word like a stopper

parts.note: a drip is a feeble, wet person, a wimp

indicators.note: regularly means taking letters at even intervals, here the second and fourth of glues

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of glues

explanation.surface: Nuns apply glue at regular intervals to stop a leak dripping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drips' looks like leaking water, but it is the insult for feeble, wet people; 'regularly' takes every other letter of glues, and 'to stop' plugs those letters inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A wimple is the cloth headdress covering the head and neck worn by many nuns.

clue.text: Game wrecked after losing bishop

indicators.note: the word has to lose the letter named

parts.note: wrecked and blotto are both slang for very drunk
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop; it is removed

explanation.surface: A player's game falls apart once the bishop is lost, as in chess.
explanation.walkthrough: The chess picture makes "wrecked" sound like a ruined position; it is slang for drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Lotto is a game of chance with numbered cards.

clue.text: Jumbo jet uncovered in the plane compound

indicators.note: uncovered means the outer letters are stripped off, leaving the middle of jet

parts.note: the middle letter of jet

indicators.note: to compound is to mix together, so the letters of these words are blended into a new order

explanation.surface: A jumbo jet, its covers off, sits in the aircraft compound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumbo jet' reads as one aircraft, but 'Jumbo' is the definition; the jet is uncovered to leave its middle E, and 'compound' mixes IN THE PLANE.
explanation.definitionFit: Jumbo means huge, and elephantine means as large as an elephant; Jumbo was also a famous elephant.

clue.text: Give up rabbit

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read from the bottom

parts.note: to give money is to pay

explanation.walkthrough: "Give up" wants to be one phrase meaning surrender. In British slang to rabbit (on) is to chatter endlessly, and so is to yap.
explanation.definitionFit: A British informal use: to rabbit on is to chatter tiresomely, and the other word is equally informal for noisy chatter.

clue.text: Crop a former PM's broadcast

indicators.note: something broadcast is heard, so go by the sound

parts.note: Theresa May was UK Prime Minister 2016 to 2019

explanation.surface: An ex-Prime Minister's interview is cut short.
explanation.walkthrough: "Crop" looks like a verb, to cut the broadcast; it is the noun, a harvest.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this cereal, also called corn, is one of the world's main field crops.

clue.text: Odd climbing gear worn by Earl's killer

indicators.note: in a down clue, climbing reads the word upwards
the Earl wears the dress, so it goes round him

parts.note: rum is British slang for odd
dress is clothing, gear
E = earl

explanation.surface: An eccentric outfit for a mountaineering aristocrat.
explanation.walkthrough: The picture is of strange climbing kit; "climbing" is really the instruction to flip RUM.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition is general: the answer is one particular kind of killer, a woman who has committed murder.

clue.text: Popular measures for auditors making cuts

definitions.note: the answer is a verb, 'incises', where the definition is the participle phrase

parts.note: in = fashionable, popular

indicators.note: auditors are listeners, so the word is judged by its sound

parts.note: sizes are measurements

explanation.surface: Accountants taking a well-liked approach to reducing spending.
explanation.walkthrough: "Auditors" and "cuts" build an accounts picture; auditors here are simply listeners.
explanation.definitionFit: To incise is to cut into something.

clue.text: Fish lists at Billingsgate

indicators.note: Billingsgate is London's fish market, where a Cockney accent drops the H

parts.note: a ship that lists heels over; the H goes

explanation.surface: Stall price lists at London's fish market.
explanation.walkthrough: Billingsgate is London's historic fish market, so a Cockney porter says 'EELS for heels. "Lists" looks like price lists; it is leaning over.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain class name: these snake-like creatures are fish, and jellied ones are a Cockney speciality, which suits Billingsgate.

clue.text: Motorway enclosed by illuminated verge

indicators.note: the first word sits inside the second

parts.note: lit = lit up, illuminated
the M1, written MI, is the classic crossword motorway

explanation.surface: A motorway with floodlit grass verges.
explanation.walkthrough: The roadside verge is a false trail: here verge means an edge or boundary.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of edge or boundary, the point beyond which you cannot go.

clue.text: Awful crime pal and I observed

indicators.note: an awful version of the letters is a bad, jumbled one

parts.note: anagram fodder; 'and' just joins

explanation.surface: A witness admits seeing a dreadful offence alongside an accomplice.
explanation.walkthrough: "Observed" reads as a verb, what the pair saw; it is an adjective, based on observation.
explanation.definitionFit: Empirical knowledge is observed rather than theorised.

clue.text: Chicken beats other birds

parts.note: chicken and yellow both mean cowardly
to beat soundly is to hammer

explanation.surface: A farmyard hen sees off rival birds.
explanation.walkthrough: "Chicken" is a bird too, hence "other birds" in the definition, but here it means cowardly. Yellowhammers are small yellow buntings.
explanation.definitionFit: Yellowhammers are birds, other than the chicken just mentioned.

clue.text: Tipsy medic using a wrong direction

indicators.note: the letters stagger about like a drinker

parts.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

explanation.surface: A drunken doctor sends someone the wrong way.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a doctor's bad advice, which is exactly what the answer means.
explanation.definitionFit: A near-literal gloss: the prefix mis- means wrong and guidance means direction.

clue.text: Ravel concert's finale in lifeless Bordeaux?

indicators.note: in tells us the letter from the concert sits inside the phrase that follows

parts.note: inert means lifeless, without movement
Bordeaux is a French wine, an example of wine, hence the question mark

indicators.note: a finale is the end, so take the last letter of concert

parts.note: the word concert, the 's only marking whose finale it is

explanation.surface: Ravel's concert ends with a flat glass of claret.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ravel' looks like the French composer, which suits the concert, but it is the verb, to tangle. The question mark flags Bordeaux as one example of WINE.
explanation.definitionFit: To ravel is to tangle or twist threads together, which is to intertwine them.

clue.text: Record store new in Greek capital, possibly

parts.note: EP = extended-play record
a silo stores grain
N = new

explanation.surface: A new record shop opening in Athens.
explanation.walkthrough: "Greek capital" wants to be Athens; it is a capital letter of the Greek alphabet, and "possibly" admits epsilon might be lower case.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsilon is a Greek letter, capital E among its forms.

clue.text: Duck's tail hurt after gents step on it

indicators.note: what follows comes after the first piece

parts.note: the gents is a men's toilet, a loo

indicators.note: a tail is the back end of an animal, so take the back end of the word

parts.note: last letter of ducK
to smart is to sting, to hurt

explanation.surface: A duck is hurt when some men tread on its tail.
explanation.walkthrough: "Step on it" seems to be the men treading on the duck; it is the idiom for hurry up. Look smart is British for be quick.
explanation.definitionFit: Look smart and step on it both mean hurry up.

clue.text: Second mate's boy comes aboard

definitions.meaning: the son of a second husband or wife
to come aboard a bus is to get on it with a stride; split the letters 5,2

explanation.surface: A second mate on a ship brings his lad on board.
explanation.walkthrough: The second mate is a ship's officer in the surface; in the answer it is a second marriage partner.
explanation.definitionFit: A stepson is the son of one's second mate; someone boarding steps on.

clue.text: Toff — one that keeps feeling capital!

indicators.note: the outer word holds the inner one

parts.note: a nob or toff is an upper-class person
an air is a feeling or atmosphere
I = one, the Roman numeral

explanation.surface: An upper-class type exclaims that it all feels splendid.
explanation.walkthrough: "Capital!" is a toff's cry of approval in the surface; it is the city, capital of Kenya. A toff is a posh person.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the answer is one capital city, Kenya's.

clue.text: Establish how a monarch passed on lies

definitions.meaning: to establish someone is to install them in a post

definitions.text: how a monarch passed on lies
definitions.meaning: a dead king or queen is laid out with ceremony so the public can pay respects; split the letters 2,5

explanation.surface: Proving how a king spread falsehoods.
explanation.walkthrough: "Passed on lies" reads as spreading falsehoods; it means died and is lying. A monarch lies in state before the funeral.
explanation.definitionFit: A double definition: the verb means to install in office, and read as two words it is the ceremonial lying of a dead monarch.

clue.text: Draw spotlight away from winning coach

parts.note: a team that is up is ahead
a stagecoach, so a stage is a coach

explanation.surface: A victorious manager is upstaged by his own publicity.
explanation.walkthrough: "Coach" reads as a sports trainer; it is the horse-drawn vehicle, a stage.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatre idiom: an actor who moves upstage makes a colleague face away from the audience, stealing the spotlight.

clue.text: Sanitised, like Troy in the Iliad, say

parts.note: as = like

indicators.note: the letter goes inside the word

parts.note: the Iliad is an example of an epic poem
T = troy, the weight system

explanation.surface: Troy, as Homer's epic portrays it, has been sanitised.
explanation.walkthrough: Troy is the city in Homer's Iliad in the surface; the wordplay only wants its abbreviation T, from troy weight.
explanation.definitionFit: Aseptic means free of germs, sanitised.

clue.text: One paying to receive American tan lingerie

indicators.note: the outer word takes the other inside

parts.note: someone who pays out
US = American
to tan someone's hide is to beat, belt, them

explanation.surface: A shopper paying for an American's tan-coloured underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: "Tan" reads as a colour of stockings; it is the verb, to thrash.
explanation.definitionFit: A suspender belt is an item of women's underwear that holds up stockings.

clue.text: Engineers left computers fired up again

parts.note: RE = Royal Engineers
L = left
IT = information technology

explanation.surface: Technicians left the computers to reboot.
explanation.walkthrough: "Fired up" suggests switching a computer on; here it is lighting a fire again.
explanation.definitionFit: Something relit has been set alight again.

clue.text: Theatre incomplete without female company

indicators.note: the last letter is missing

parts.note: the stage means the theatre as a profession; drop the E

explanation.surface: An unfinished play staged with no women in the cast.
explanation.walkthrough: A stag party or stag night is a men-only celebration before a wedding.
explanation.definitionFit: Stag describes an all-male occasion, without women.

clue.text: Open-air café of note next to a grand forest

parts.note: te is a note of the sol-fa scale
A as printed
G = grand, a thousand
the Forest of Arden, from As You Like It

explanation.surface: A notable outdoor café beside a great forest.
explanation.walkthrough: "Of note" reads as famous; it is the musical note TE. "Grand" looks like an adjective for the forest; it is G.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain description: the answer names a garden where refreshments are served outdoors, which is what an open-air café is.

clue.text: Money mostly for parties

indicators.note: most of the word: drop its last letter

parts.note: dosh is British slang for money; the H goes

explanation.surface: Cash spent largely on partying.
explanation.walkthrough: A do is a British word for a party, and dosh is British slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: A British informal use: a do is a party or social function, and the plural matches parties.

clue.text: Sort of hilt round a heavy Indian club

indicators.note: a sorted, rearranged version of the letters
the rearranged letters go round A

parts.note: HILT rearranged
A as printed, placed inside

explanation.surface: A sword hilt wrapped around an Indian weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: A lathi is the long iron-bound bamboo stick carried by Indian police.
explanation.definitionFit: A lathi is a heavy stick used as a club in India.

clue.text: Huge jar in the auditorium

indicators.note: an auditorium is where things are heard

parts.note: to jar is to grate on the nerves

explanation.surface: An enormous jar standing in a concert hall.
explanation.walkthrough: "Jar" reads as a pot; it is the verb, to grate.
explanation.definitionFit: Great and huge both mean very large.

clue.text: In retrospect, a clean World Cup, perhaps

indicators.note: the answer is inside the words that follow

parts.note: retroSPECT A CLEan

explanation.surface: Looking back, a World Cup free of scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: "Perhaps" marks the World Cup as just one example of a spectacle.
explanation.definitionFit: A World Cup is a grand public show, a spectacle.
